# Bf-Tree

Bf-Tree is a modern read-write-optimized concurrent larger-than-memory range index in Rust from MSR.

## Design Details

You can find the Bf-Tree research paper [here](https://badrish.net/papers/bftree-vldb2024.pdf). You can find more design docs [here](/doc).
## User Guide

### Rust

Bf-Tree is written in Rust, and is available as a Rust crate. You can add Bf-Tree to your `Cargo.toml` like this:
```bash
$ cargo add bf_tree
```
Which will add bf_tree as a dependency to your Cargo.toml
```toml
[dependencies]
bf-tree = "0.5.7"
```

An example use of Bf-Tree:

```rust
use bf_tree::BfTree;
use bf_tree::LeafReadResult;

let mut config = bf_tree::Config::default();
config.cb_min_record_size(4);
let tree = BfTree::with_config(config, None).unwrap();
tree.insert(b"key", b"value");

let mut buffer = [0u8; 1024];
let read_size = tree.read(b"key", &mut buffer);

assert_eq!(read_size, LeafReadResult::Found(5));
assert_eq!(&buffer[..5], b"value");
```

### Configuration

Start with `Config::default()`, customize it with builder-style setters such as
`config.cb_size_byte(64 * 1024 * 1024)`. Validate the configuration with
`config.validate()?` before passing it to `BfTree::with_config(config, None)`.
`BfTree::with_config` also validates it internally and returns a `ConfigError`
if it is invalid. Defaults below refer to `Config::default()`.
Record sizes are the combined key and value lengths in bytes, excluding metadata.

#### Buffer Pool

The circular buffer holds cached mini pages and full pages. Its size is not a
limit on total process memory: inner nodes, page mappings, and any in-memory
backing storage require additional memory.

| Parameter | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cb_size_byte` | 32 MiB | Circular-buffer capacity in bytes; must be a power of two. |
| `cb_min_record_size` | 4 | Minimum record size in bytes; must be at least 2. Inserts with smaller records are rejected. |
| `cb_max_record_size` | 1952 | Maximum record size in bytes. Inserts with larger records are rejected; increasing this limit must also satisfy page-layout constraints. |
| `cb_max_key_len` | 16 | Maximum key length in bytes. Set this to accommodate the longest key in your workload. |
| `read_promotion_rate` | 30% (50% in debug builds) | Probability of promoting a record into the buffer during a point read. |
| `scan_promotion_rate` | 30% (50% in debug builds) | Probability of promoting a page into the buffer during a range scan. Lower values help avoid displacing hot data with scan results. |

Promotion rates are percentages from 0 to 100: 0 disables the corresponding
promotion, while 100 always attempts it when eligible.

#### Persistent Storage

These settings control the backing store and how reads populate its cache.
The promotion rates are listed again here because they also affect storage I/O.

| Parameter | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read_promotion_rate` | 30% (50% in debug builds) | Controls caching on point reads; higher rates can reduce repeated backing-store reads at the cost of more cache churn. |
| `scan_promotion_rate` | 30% (50% in debug builds) | Controls page caching during scans; lower rates reduce cache pollution from one-pass scans. |
| `storage_backend` | `StorageBackend::Memory` | Backing-store implementation. `Memory` keeps backing pages in RAM; `Std` uses standard file I/O. Linux additionally supports `StdDirect`, `IoUringPolling`, and `IoUringBlocking`; `Spdk` requires Linux and the `spdk` feature. |
| `file_path` | Empty path | Index-file path for file-backed storage. Set this together with a file-backed `storage_backend`; changing the path alone does not change the backend. |
| `cache_only` | `false` | Keeps all leaf data in the circular buffer, without a backing storage layer. The entire dataset must fit in the buffer. This differs from `StorageBackend::Memory`, which normally keeps backing pages in separately allocated RAM. |

As a convenience, `Config::new(path, buffer_size)` selects `Std` for a normal
file path, `Memory` for a path starting with `:memory:`, or cache-only mode for
a path starting with `:cache:`. File-backed storage alone does not provide
snapshot recovery; see the snapshot options below.

#### Snapshot & Recovery

| Parameter | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `snapshot_backend` | `StorageBackend::Std` | I/O backend used to write snapshots, separate from the index's `storage_backend`. This is currently crate-internal and has no public setter. |
| `use_snapshot` | `false` | Enables concurrent consistent snapshots. Call `BfTree::cpr_snapshot` explicitly to take one; enabling this does not schedule automatic snapshots. |
| `snapshot_version` | 0 | Initial snapshot version for a new tree. Normally leave this unchanged; recovery automatically starts at the saved version plus one. |
### C and C++ interface

The [unreleased C ABI package](bf-tree-ffi/README.md) wraps the existing Rust
operations with caller-owned buffers, explicit statuses, bounded scans, and
panic fencing. It preserves ABI-v1 layouts and signatures.
The native read, scan, mutation, and snapshot implementations remain unchanged.
Recovery validation uses two additional read-only `Config` getters.

### Snapshots and Recovery

Bf-Tree supports CPR-style consistent snapshots. A snapshot captures a
consistent prefix of all in-flight transactions to a file, and a tree can later
be reconstructed from such a snapshot file.

To enable snapshots, set `use_snapshot(true)` on the `Config` before creating
the tree. Once enabled, call [`BfTree::cpr_snapshot`] with the destination path
to take a snapshot at any point. Snapshots can be taken concurrently with
ongoing reads and writes; only one snapshot may be in progress at a time.

To recover a tree from a snapshot file, use
[`BfTree::new_from_cpr_snapshot`]. The snapshot file embeds most configuration
fields (record sizes, leaf page size, cache-only flag, etc.), so the caller
only needs to specify the recovery-time options:

- `recovery_snapshot_file_path`: path of the snapshot file to recover from.
- `use_snapshot`: whether the recovered tree should itself support taking new
  snapshots.
- `buffer_ptr`: optional pointer to a pre-allocated cache buffer; pass `None`
  to let Bf-Tree allocate one.
- `buffer_size`: optional override of the cache size stored in the snapshot.
  If smaller than the original, recovery may fail because cached pages from
  the snapshot must fit in memory.
- `wal`: optional write-ahead log configuration for the recovered tree.

```rust
use bf_tree::{BfTree, Config};
use std::path::PathBuf;

let mut config = Config::default();
config.use_snapshot(true);
let tree = BfTree::with_config(config, None).unwrap();

tree.insert(b"key", b"value");

// Take a CPR snapshot of the current tree state.
tree.cpr_snapshot("snapshot.bftree");

// Recover a bf-tree from a CPR snapshot
let tree = BfTree::new_from_cpr_snapshot(
    "snapshot.bftree",
    /* use_snapshot */ true,
    /* buffer_ptr */ None,
    /* buffer_size */ None,
    /* wal */ None,
).unwrap();
std::fs::remove_file("snapshot.bftree");
```

You can check whether all active threads have transitioned to the next
snapshot version during a snapshot (i.e., all threads are operating in v + 1) with:

```rust,ignore
let ready = tree.are_all_threads_in_next_snapshot_version();
```

This is useful for coordinating external systems that need to wait until a
snapshot's data is fully consistent but not the whole snapshot to finish
before proceeding. Note that, this function returns false if no ongoing snapshot.

Notes:
- The snapshot file path passed to `cpr_snapshot` must be different from the
  path used by any concurrent recovery.
- For more on the snapshot/recovery design, see
  [doc/snapshot-recovery.md](doc/snapshot-recovery.md).

PRs are accepted and preferred over feature requests. Feel free to reach out if you have any design questions.

## Developer Guide

### Building

#### Prerequisite

Bf-Tree supports Linux, Windows, and macOS, although only a recently version of Linux is rigorously tested. Bf-Tree is written in Rust, which you can install [here](https://rustup.rs).

Please install pre-commit hooks to ensure that your code is formatted and linted in the same way as the rest of the project; the coding style will be enforced in CI, these hooks act as a pre-filter.

```bash
# If on Ubuntu
sudo apt update && sudo apt install pre-commit
pre-commit install
```

#### Build

```bash
cargo build --release
```

### Testing

#### Unit Tests

```bash
cargo test
```

Circular-buffer free-list reuse has a deterministic spurious-CAS regression.
It exercises the production allocator with a test-only atomic wrapper and
checks reuse and eviction without relying on hardware producing a spurious
failure. Separate integration tests use native atomics for repeated reuse and
capacity-pressure/wraparound coverage:

```bash
cargo test --lib circular_buffer
cargo test --test circular_buffer_reuse
```

The injector is disabled with `shuttle`; Shuttle tests continue to use Shuttle's
atomics. Free-list allocation must not abandon an unlinked entry on a spurious
CAS failure, since eviction cannot remove that orphan from the list.

#### Reliability Tests

The native suite also covers stateful operations against an ordered-map model,
bounded linearizability checking, scans overlapping mutations and splits,
resource lifecycle accounting, process-crash snapshot recovery, malformed
snapshots, and WAL write failures. These complement the allocator and traversal
regressions rather than replacing them.

```bash
cargo test --release --lib -- stateful_tree linearizability concurrent_scans
# Linux: run exact file-descriptor/thread accounting without parallel tests.
env BFTREE_RESOURCE_CHECK=1 cargo test --release --lib resource_lifecycle -- --test-threads=1
```

CI additionally runs deterministic fuzz regressions, AddressSanitizer with leak
detection, selected Shuttle schedules, and focused Miri checks.

#### Shuttle Tests

Concurrent systems are nondeterministic, and subject to exponential amount of different thread interleaving. We use [shuttle](https://github.com/awslabs/shuttle)
to deterministically and systematically explore different thread interleaving to uncover the bugs caused by subtle multithread interactions.

```bash
# Core Bf-tree concurrent operations (~5 minutes)
cargo test --features "shuttle" --release shuttle_bf_tree_concurrent_operations

# CPR snapshot with disk-backed storage (fast, < 1s)
cargo test --features "shuttle" --release shuttle_cpr_snapshot_disk

# CPR snapshot with cache-only (in-memory) storage
cargo test --features "shuttle" --release shuttle_cpr_snapshot_cache_only
```

To replay a specific failing schedule (generated automatically on failure into `target/schedule000.txt`):

```bash
cargo test --features "shuttle" --release shuttle_replay -- --nocapture
```

#### Fuzz Tests

Fuzz testing is a bug finding technique that generates random inputs to the system and test for crash. Bf-Tree employs fuzzing to generate random operation sequences
(e.g., insert, read, scan) to the system and check that none of the operation sequence will crash the system or lead to inconsistent state. Check the 
[fuzz](fuzz/README.md) folder for more details.

#### Production Stress Matrix

On November 1, 2026, a production-stress campaign completed **2,744 cases with
zero failures**. It included 56 warmup cases and four rounds of 672 cases, using both
release builds and release builds with debug assertions and overflow checks.

Each full round covered three value-size profiles, four memory-budget labels
(minimum, double-minimum, quarter-data, and data), seven read/write/scan mixes,
and eight worker counts: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 36, 72, and 144. Full cases used 262,144 records and a
30-second workload; warmups used 65,536 records and 15 seconds. Preload,
verification, drain, and teardown time were additional.

Production Stress Matrix

On November 1, 2026, a production-stress campaign completed 2,744 cases with zero failures. It included 56 warmup cases and four rounds of 672 cases, using both release builds and release builds with debug assertions and overflow checks.

Each full round covered three value-size profiles, four memory-budget labels (minimum, double-minimum, quarter-data, and data), seven read/write/scan mixes, and eight worker counts: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 36, 72, and 144. Full cases used 262,144 records and a 30-second workload; warmups used 65,536 records and 15 seconds. Preload, verification, drain, and teardown time were additional.

Seeds, scan lengths, contention, full-page caching, build profiles, and storage backends (io_uring polling/blocking, direct I/O, and standard file I/O) rotated across groups and rounds. This was production-stress coverage, not an exhaustive Cartesian product of every setting or a platform/feature compatibility matrix. Each passing case checked final point reads, a full scan, draining, and a second full scan, and completed tree teardown.

The regular suite retains fast parameterized stress cases. A separate ignored test accepts a JSON configuration for longer runs:

cargo test --release --lib production_mixed_record_stress
# Bash: run one standalone timed case, not the full supervised campaign.
env BF_PRODUCTION_CASE='{"seed":42,"records":262144,"threads":8,"seconds":30,"backend":"std","memory_bytes":1048576}' \
    cargo test --release --lib tests::production_stress::production_matrix_case -- --exact --ignored --nocapture

Omitted JSON fields use the defaults in src/tests/production_stress.rs. The campaign's external supervisor was configured to capture three GDB full-thread backtraces, process snapshots, and a core dump on stalls, then hold the original process for diagnosis. It used a 60-second workload no-progress trigger and 660-720-second whole-case diagnostic deadlines, with no overall campaign timeout. Timeouts, missing results, and zero-test runs were not counted as passes. The standalone command above does not provide that supervision.

Benchmarking

Check the benchmark folder for more details.

cd benchmark
env SHUMAI_FILTER="inmemory" MIMALLOC_LARGE_OS_PAGES=1 cargo run --bin bftree --release

More advanced benchmarking, with metrics collecting, numa-node binding, huge page, etc:

env MIMALLOC_SHOW_STATS=1 MIMALLOC_LARGE_OS_PAGES=1 MIMALLOC_RESERVE_HUGE_OS_PAGES_AT=0 numactl --membind=0 --cpunodebind=0 cargo bench --features "metrics-rt" micro

aiSummary.oneLiner: A read-write-optimized, concurrent, larger-than-memory range index written in Rust.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: Bf-Tree is a highly advanced, read-write-optimized range index data structure developed by Microsoft Research and implemented entirely in modern Rust. It is specifically engineered to manage massive, larger-than-memory datasets efficiently by utilizing a highly concurrent, tree-based architecture. The system minimizes expensive disk I/O operations by tightly optimizing its internal node layouts to align with modern CPU caches, drastically reducing latency during complex search operations. It employs sophisticated lock-free techniques to allow thousands of threads to query and mutate the index simultaneously without experiencing performance-degrading contention. As an open-source crate, it serves as a foundational building block for developers creating high-throughput database engines and specialized storage systems.
keyFeatures: Larger-Than-Memory Indexing: Efficiently manages and queries massive datasets that far exceed the available RAM by intelligently paging data to disk.
Read-Write Optimized Architecture: Balances the structural design to ensure that heavy data insertion workloads do not significantly degrade query read speeds.
Highly Concurrent Operations: Implements advanced lock-free algorithms to allow massive multi-threaded access without traditional locking bottlenecks.
Native Rust Implementation: Written entirely in safe, modern Rust, guaranteeing memory safety and high performance across various computing platforms.
CPU Cache Alignment: Carefully structures internal B-tree nodes to maximize cache locality, significantly reducing expensive main memory fetches.
Modular Crate Distribution: Packaged standardly via Cargo, allowing developers to easily integrate the advanced indexing engine into their existing Rust projects.

useCases.title: Building Next-Gen Database Engines
useCases.description: Database architects can replace their legacy indexing structures with Bf-Tree to instantly increase the transactional throughput of their custom storage engines.

useCases.title: High-Performance File Systems
useCases.description: OS developers can implement this data structure to manage vast directory hierarchies and metadata indexing efficiently on modern NVMe storage arrays.

useCases.title: Large-Scale Telemetry Processing
useCases.description: Engineers can index millions of incoming IoT sensor events per second concurrently without experiencing thread contention bottlenecks.

useCases.title: Real-Time Financial Trading Systems
useCases.description: Quantitative developers can utilize the concurrent data structure to manage massive, high-frequency order books with absolute minimal latency.

useCases.title: In-Memory Caching Layers
useCases.description: Backend teams can build incredibly fast key-value stores that gracefully handle massive datasets by spilling over to disk intelligently.

aiSummary.whoIsItFor: This library is designed for systems programmers, database engineers, and researchers building high-performance storage infrastructure. It requires a strong understanding of concurrent programming and Rust.
